idiom_name: final case class Interval[A](lo: Option[A], hi: Option[A], loClosed: Boolean, hiClosed: Boolean)
implementation_notes: Without extra dependencies the pattern is a final case class over a typeclass-ordered A: Option endpoints encode open ends (None = unbounded), two booleans encode inclusivity, and require (or Either) in the constructor enforces that the lower endpoint does not exceed the upper. scala.math.Ordering supplies the comparisons and named constructors in the companion object (closed, closedOpen, atLeast, atMost) keep call sites declarative. Note that scala.collection.immutable.Range is a different thing - it enumerates Int/Long/BigInt values and is not an interval value over an arbitrary domain.
pitfalls: scala.collection.immutable.Range (1 to 10) looks like the pattern and is not: it enumerates integers, cannot represent an empty or open interval, and importing it accidentally shadows the domain type.
Option endpoints make None mean unbounded, but None is also what a defaulted field holds: Interval(hi = Some(end)) builds an open-ended range by accident in a case class with defaults.

Ordering[A] must be consistent with equals for interval equality, set membership and map keys to agree; a custom Ordering that disagrees with equals yields intervals that are equal in one sense and distinct in another.

A case class with a second parameter list does not give the usual copy/equality conveniences over the implicit ordering, and require failures surface only at runtime - validate at construction, not at use.

variants.name: spire.math.Interval (explicit bound kinds, algebra)
variants.implementation_notes: spire.math.Interval is the most complete Scala realization: each bound kind is explicit (Closed, Open, Unbound, plus the empty interval), constructors cover closed, open, openLower, openUpper, above, below, atOrAbove, atOrBelow, all and empty, and the API offers contains, intersects, intersect, union, isSubsetOf/isSupersetOf, meet and join. It needs an Order[A] instance and pulls in the Typelevel algebra stack, which is why a dependency-free case class remains a reasonable default when the project only needs one value object.
variants.code_sketch:
import spire.math.Interval

val billing   = Interval.openUpper(d1, d2)     // [d1, d2)
val openEnded = Interval.atOrAbove(d1)         // [d1, +inf)

billing.contains(today)
billing.intersects(usage)
Interval.closed(1, 10) meet Interval.closed(5, 20)   // [5, 10]
pitfalls: Every operation needs an implicit Order[A]; with the wrong instance the interval silently orders by a different field than the domain intends.
The empty interval is a first-class result of meet/intersection, so callers must handle it instead of assuming a non-empty overlap.
Constructors silently collapse invalid input: closed(5, 1) is the empty interval rather than an error, which hides what is usually a domain bug.
